parallel.problem: When a population of identical supercooled water droplets is cooled, why do a few stay liquid far below the temperature at which most freeze?
parallel.how_studied: Researchers repeatedly freeze and thaw the same droplets in microfluidic arrays or on cold stages. This tests whether the same droplets freeze at the same temperature every cycle ('singular' hypothesis: a fixed particle or site causes it) or at random temperatures ('stochastic' hypothesis). It parallels the Luria–Delbrück fluctuation test. Hold-at-constant-temperature experiments then measure freezing-rate statistics, and electron microscopy identifies any nucleating particles.

<parallel>
Field: Atmospheric physics (ice nucleation)
Problem: When a population of identical supercooled water droplets is cooled, why do a few stay liquid far below the temperature at which most freeze?
How it is studied: Researchers repeatedly freeze and thaw the same droplets in microfluidic arrays or on cold stages. This tests whether the same droplets freeze at the same temperature every cycle ('singular' hypothesis: a fixed particle or site causes it) or at random temperatures ('stochastic' hypothesis). Each of your ideas must transfer a specific method, measurement logic, or principle from how that field studies its problem, while still being a concrete, scientifically sound way to address the research question.

Research question: "What measurements or analyses would best reveal why a small fraction of genetically identical cancer cells survive targeted drug treatment?"

Propose 5 distinct, concrete ideas (analyses, measurements, or experiments) that a research lab could pursue to address this question. For each idea give a short title and a description of one or two sentences.

ideas.title: Constant-dose kill-kinetics analysis (isothermal hold analog)
ideas.description: Hold cell populations at a fixed drug concentration and measure the death rate over time using live-cell imaging. A single-exponential decay points to a uniform stochastic hazard, while a biphasic curve with a plateau points to a pre-existing subpopulation with a lower hazard.

ideas.title: Luria–Delbrück fluctuation test across many small subclones
ideas.description: Expand many independent subclones, each started from a few cells, for different numbers of generations, then treat them in parallel and compare how much the survivor counts vary from clone to clone. Variance near Poisson suggests drug-induced or random survival. Very high variance suggests pre-existing survivor states, and how it changes with expansion time gives the rate at which cells switch into and out of that state.

ideas.title: Dose-ramp survival spectrum (freezing-spectrum analog)
ideas.description: Measure the fraction of cells surviving across a fine range of drug concentrations and convert it into a cumulative density of resistance-conferring states per cell, similar to how ice-nucleation work builds an active-site spectrum. Compare these spectra between cell lines and growth conditions to test whether a fixed, quantifiable cellular feature sets the tail.

ideas.title: Retrospective lineage barcoding to identify the 'nucleating particle'
ideas.description: Label cells with expressed lineage barcodes, split the population, treat one half, and use single-cell RNA and ATAC sequencing on the untreated twin half to profile the pre-treatment state of the lineages that later survived. This works like electron microscopy finding the particle responsible for freezing: it identifies the specific molecular feature linked to survival.

ideas.title: Remove the putative site and re-test (site-deactivation control)
ideas.description: Use FACS to deplete, or CRISPR to knock down, the candidate marker found in idea 4 (for example, high expression of a drug-efflux or stress-response gene) before treatment, then check whether the low-survival tail disappears or comes back. This is like heat-treating samples to destroy nucleating sites, and it tests whether the feature actually causes survival.
